Read the first three rows as physics rather than as bookkeeping. The hypothesis in row one is that the laws are the same at every moment. The hypothesis in row two is that they are the same at every place. The hypothesis in row three is that they are the same in every direction. So:

What the classical conservation laws are actually about

Momentum is conserved because space is uniform. Energy is conserved because time is uniform. Angular momentum is conserved because space is isotropic.

None of these is a fact about matter. You cannot invent a new particle, or a new force, or a new material, that violates them — as long as it lives in a uniform, isotropic space and an unchanging time, its action has those symmetries and the charges are conserved whatever else it does. Conversely, the only way to break one is to break the corresponding symmetry, and §4 shows three situations where that genuinely happens. This is why conservation laws survived the transitions to relativity and quantum mechanics untouched while nearly everything else about mechanics was rewritten: they were never claims about mechanics in the first place.

In plain terms 1.4.3

Energy, momentum and angular momentum arrive here as one calculation performed three times with different entries. Shift every clock by the same amount and, provided the scalar has no explicit dependence on the time, the conserved quantity is the energy. Shift every particle by the same displacement and, provided the potential depends only on separations, it is the total momentum. Turn everything through one angle about an axis and, provided the potential depends only on the lengths of those separations, it is the angular momentum about it.

Read as physics rather than bookkeeping, the three hypotheses say the laws are the same at every moment, the same at every place, and the same in every direction. Three separate empirical laws have become one statement about the uniformity of the arena. None is a fact about matter, and no particle, force or material can be invented that violates them, because so long as it lives in a uniform isotropic space and an unchanging time its scalar carries those symmetries and the quantities are conserved whatever else it does.

Notice what has replaced the third law. Momentum conservation followed there from an assumption that internal forces cancel in pairs; it follows here from the observation that a potential between two bodies can depend only on how far apart they are — the same physical content, no longer an axiom about forces.

4 · When symmetry fails, conservation fails

A theorem earns trust by being falsifiable. If symmetry really is the reason for conservation, then removing the symmetry must remove the conservation law — and remove that one only, leaving the others intact. This section takes the theorem at its word.

4.1 · The rate at which conservation fails

Start with the quantitative version, which is stronger than "the theorem no longer applies". Differentiate E=∑ipiq˙i−LE=\sum_{i}p_{i}\dot q_{i}-LE=∑i​pi​q˙​i​−L along a solution, with LLL now allowed an explicit ttt-dependence:

dEdt=∑i[p˙iq˙i+piq¨i]−∑i[∂L∂qiq˙i+∂L∂q˙iq¨i]−∂L∂t=∑iq˙i[p˙i−∂L∂qi]⏟= 0 on shell+∑iq¨i[pi−∂L∂q˙i]⏟= 0 by definition−∂L∂t, \begin{aligned} \dv{E}{t} &= \sum_{i}\Big[\dot p_{i}\dot q_{i} + p_{i}\ddot q_{i}\Big] - \sum_{i}\left[\pdv{L}{q_{i}}\dot q_{i} + \pdv{L}{\dot q_{i}}\ddot q_{i}\right] - \pdv{L}{t}\\[4pt] &= \sum_{i}\dot q_{i}\underbrace{\left[\dot p_{i} - \pdv{L}{q_{i}}\right]}_{=\,0\ \text{on shell}} + \sum_{i}\ddot q_{i}\underbrace{\left[p_{i}-\pdv{L}{\dot q_{i}}\right]}_{=\,0\ \text{by definition}} - \pdv{L}{t}, \end{aligned} dtdE​​=i∑​[p˙​i​q˙​i​+pi​q¨​i​]−i∑​[∂qi​∂L​q˙​i​+∂q˙​i​∂L​q¨​i​]−∂t∂L​=i∑​q˙​i​=0 on shell[p˙​i​−∂qi​∂L​]​​+i∑​q¨​i​=0 by definition[pi​−∂q˙​i​∂L​]​​−∂t∂L​,​ (1.4.26)
  dEdt  =  −∂L∂t.   \boxed{\;\dv{E}{t} \;=\; -\pdv{L}{t}.\;} dtdE​=−∂t∂L​.​ (1.4.27)

Read that as an accounting identity. The left side is the rate at which the conservation law is violated; the right side is the rate at which the symmetry is violated. They are equal. Noether's theorem is the special case in which both sides are zero.

Example. A mass on a spring being driven by an external agent, L=12mx˙2−12kx2+x f(t)L=\half m\dot x^{2}-\half kx^{2}+x\,f(t)L=21​mx˙2−21​kx2+xf(t), has ∂L/∂t=xf˙\partial L/\partial t = x\dot f∂L/∂t=xf˙​, so dEdt=−xf˙(t)\dv{E}{t}=-x\dot f(t)dtdE​=−xf˙​(t). The energy of the oscillator is not conserved, and it should not be: something outside the system is doing work on it. The Lagrangian's explicit ttt-dependence is the mathematical signature of "there is an outside". Enlarge the system to include whatever is driving fff, and the enlarged LLL has no explicit ttt, and total energy is conserved again. Every apparent violation of energy conservation in ordinary physics is this: an incomplete system.

4.2 · A crystal: continuous symmetry broken to discrete

Now a case where the symmetry is not destroyed but reduced. An electron moving through a crystal lattice sees a potential that repeats:

V(x+a)  =  V(x)for every lattice vector a, V(\vv x + \vv a) \;=\; V(\vv x) \qquad\text{for every lattice vector }\vv a, V(x+a)=V(x)for every lattice vector a, (1.4.28)

but V(x+δ)≠V(x)V(\vv x+\vv\delta)\neq V(\vv x)V(x+δ)=V(x) for a general small displacement δ\vv\deltaδ. Translation invariance survives only for a discrete set of displacements.

Noether's theorem has nothing to say. Its hypothesis was a family q(t,ϵ)q(t,\epsilon)q(t,ϵ) continuous in ϵ\epsilonϵ, so that ∂/∂ϵ\partial/\partial\epsilon∂/∂ϵ exists at ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0; a discrete symmetry has no ϵ\epsilonϵ to differentiate with respect to, and there is no generator KKK to put into (1.4.15). And indeed momentum is not conserved: the lattice exerts forces on the electron, and p\vv pp changes.

⚑ What survives is quoted, not derived here, and belongs to solid-state physics: because the symmetry group is still nontrivial, the eigenstates can be labelled by a quantity ℏk\hbar\vv kℏk called the crystal momentum, and it is conserved modulo a reciprocal lattice vector G\vv GG — collisions can change k\vv kk by any G\vv GG at no cost. The pattern is general and worth carrying: a continuous symmetry gives an additively conserved quantity taking values in R\RR; breaking it to a discrete subgroup leaves a quantity conserved only up to the discrete "dual" of that subgroup. The residual freedom is exactly the amount of symmetry you threw away.

4.3 · An expanding universe: no conserved total energy

The striking case, and the one where the honest answer is more interesting than the tidy one.

⚑ Quoting forward to Chapter 3.8: on the largest scales the universe is well described by a spacetime whose spatial distances all grow by a common factor a(t)a(t)a(t), the scale factor. Matter fields living in that spacetime have an action whose Lagrangian contains a(t)a(t)a(t) explicitly. So ∂L/∂t≠0\partial L/\partial t\neq0∂L/∂t=0 — not because of some external driving agent that could be absorbed into a larger system, but because the geometry itself is time-dependent.

By (1.4.27) there is then no conserved energy, and this is not a technicality that a cleverer definition repairs. The most visible consequence is one you have heard described in a misleading way. Light from a distant galaxy arrives redshifted: its wavelength has been stretched by the factor aaa, so each photon's energy has fallen by 1/a1/a1/a. The energy is not transferred to the expansion, and it is not stored anywhere. There is no conserved global energy in this spacetime for it to be a part of, so there is nothing that needs to balance. Asking where it went presupposes the very conservation law that the absence of time-translation symmetry has removed.

⚠ Say exactly this much and no more

Three claims, in decreasing order of confidence.

What is certainly true. ⚑ In a general curved spacetime there is no time-translation symmetry, hence no Noether charge for it, hence no meaningful "total energy of the universe". Chapter 3.5 makes this precise: the symmetries of a spacetime are its Killing vector fields, a conserved energy requires a timelike one, and the expanding solutions of Chapter 3.8 do not have one. Killing vectors turn out to be Noether's theorem written geometrically, which is why that chapter is where this loose end gets tied.

What survives. ⚑ The local statement does hold, always and exactly: ∇μTμν=0\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}=0∇μ​Tμν=0, the covariant version of Chapter 0.7's continuity equation for the energy–momentum tensor. Energy and momentum are not created or destroyed at any point. But covariant conservation cannot be integrated over a large region to give a constant the way ∂μJμ=0\partial_{\mu}J^{\mu}=0∂μ​Jμ=0 can — the extra connection terms of Chapter 3.3 obstruct exactly that step, and ν\nuν is a free index, so the object you would like to add up is a vector at each point and there is no coordinate-free way to add vectors at different points on a curved manifold (Chapter 3.2). Local conservation is real; global conservation is a boundary condition, and here the boundary conditions are not available.

What is true only sometimes. ⚑ In spacetimes that are asymptotically flat — an isolated star, a black hole in an otherwise empty universe — the symmetry is restored far away, and a conserved total energy can be defined (the ADM mass). The expanding universe is not of this type. So "energy conservation fails in general relativity" is too strong, and "energy is always conserved, you just have to look harder" is false. The correct statement is the one Noether's theorem hands you directly: you get a conserved energy exactly when you have a time-translation symmetry, and not otherwise.

4.4 · Breaking one symmetry at a time

The figure below is the theorem's own falsification test. A particle orbits in a central potential; two dials sit next to it, and each breaks exactly one symmetry.

The system is a particle of mass mmm in the plane, with

V(r,θ,t)  =  12mω2r2 (1+λcos⁡2θ) (1+μsin⁡Ωt). V(r,\theta,t) \;=\; \half m\omega^{2}r^{2}\,\big(1+\lambda\cos 2\theta\big)\,\big(1+\mu\sin\Omega t\big). V(r,θ,t)=21​mω2r2(1+λcos2θ)(1+μsinΩt). (1.4.29)

At λ=μ=0\lambda=\mu=0λ=μ=0 this is the isotropic harmonic oscillator: rotationally symmetric, so LzL_{z}Lz​ is conserved, and time-independent, so EEE is conserved. The dial λ\lambdaλ squashes the potential into an ellipse — rotational symmetry gone, time-translation symmetry untouched. The dial μ\muμ makes the whole well breathe in time — time-translation symmetry gone, rotational symmetry untouched.

Before looking, extract a prediction. The angular equation of motion is ddt(mr2θ˙)=−∂V/∂θ\dv{}{t}\big(mr^{2}\dot\theta\big)=-\partial V/\partial\thetadtd​(mr2θ˙)=−∂V/∂θ, and mr2θ˙=Lzmr^{2}\dot\theta = L_{z}mr2θ˙=Lz​, so

dLzdt  =  −∂V∂θ  =  λ  mω2r2sin⁡2θ  (1+μsin⁡Ωt), \dv{L_{z}}{t} \;=\; -\pdv{V}{\theta} \;=\; \lambda\;m\omega^{2}r^{2}\sin 2\theta\;\big(1+\mu\sin\Omega t\big), dtdLz​​=−∂θ∂V​=λmω2r2sin2θ(1+μsinΩt), (1.4.30)

while (1.4.27) gives

dEdt  =  ∂V∂t  =  μ Ωcos⁡Ωt  ⋅12mω2r2(1+λcos⁡2θ). \dv{E}{t} \;=\; \pdv{V}{t} \;=\; \mu\,\Omega\cos\Omega t\;\cdot\half m\omega^{2}r^{2}\big(1+\lambda\cos2\theta\big). dtdE​=∂t∂V​=μΩcosΩt⋅21​mω2r2(1+λcos2θ). (1.4.31)

Each rate is exactly proportional to its own dial and completely independent of the other. The theorem does not merely predict that conservation fails; it predicts which one fails, and how fast.

One detail in the figure repays attention. At λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 the orbit is a closed ellipse; the particle retraces its own path exactly. Turn λ\lambdaλ up and the ellipse begins to precess and the path never closes. Closure of orbits is not a generic property — it is a symptom of extra conserved quantities, and Worked example 2 is about the most famous case of that.

In plain terms 1.4.4

A theorem earns trust by being falsifiable, and this one is easy to put on trial. Differentiate the energy along a solution while assuming nothing, and out comes the statement that its rate of change is exactly minus the rate at which the scalar depends on the time. The left side is how fast the conservation law fails, the right side how fast the symmetry fails, and they are the same number.

An oscillator driven from outside has a scalar depending on the time, and its energy is not conserved, because something outside is doing work on it. Explicit time dependence is the mathematical signature of there being an outside, and enlarging the system to include whatever drives it restores the symmetry and the law together. Every ordinary violation of energy conservation is an incomplete system.

One case is not of that kind, and there the honest answer beats the tidy one. On the largest scales every distance grows by a common factor depending on the time, so the geometry itself is time-dependent and there is nowhere larger to escape into. Light from a distant galaxy arrives stretched, each photon carrying less energy than it set out with, and that energy has not been transferred or stored anywhere, because no conserved global energy exists for it to belong to. Asking where it went assumes the law the missing symmetry removed.

5 · Discrete symmetries — an honest exception

Nature has symmetries that are not continuous, and the theorem simply does not reach them. The three that matter are parity PPP (reflect all spatial coordinates, x→−x\vv x\to-\vv xx→−x), charge conjugation CCC (exchange every particle for its antiparticle), and time reversal TTT (t→−tt\to-tt→−t). None of them can be applied a little bit. Parity is the cleanest case to see why: the matrix −I-I−I has determinant −1-1−1 in three dimensions, the identity has determinant +1+1+1, and the determinant of a rotation-or- reflection is a continuous function taking only those two values — so no continuous path of transformations connects PPP to the identity without leaving the group. There is therefore no one-parameter family to differentiate: no ϵ\epsilonϵ, no generator KKK, no (1.4.15), and no conserved current. What a discrete symmetry gives instead — and only in quantum mechanics, where states can be eigenvectors of the operation — is a multiplicative quantum number, typically ±1\pm1±1, whose product over the particles present is the same before and after a reaction. Additive charges come from continuous symmetries; multiplicative ones from discrete symmetries. They are different objects with different arithmetic.

⚑ Quoted, and developed in Chapter 6.6: both PPP and CPCPCP are violated in nature. Parity was found to fail in the weak interaction in 1957, and the combination CPCPCP was found to fail in 1964. This was a genuine surprise, and it is instructive about how much of physics is convention and how much is fact — nobody had ever suspected that the laws could distinguish left from right, because there is no reason within mechanics or electromagnetism why they should. There is no Noether charge to lose, and correspondingly no continuity equation quietly breaks; the symmetry just is not there. The one combination that appears to survive is CPTCPTCPT, and ⚑ that one is not an accident — it is a theorem, forced by Lorentz invariance and locality, which is why it has a different status from the others.

In plain terms 1.4.5

Some of nature's symmetries cannot be applied a little at a time, and the theorem does not reach them. Reflecting every spatial direction is the clean case: that operation and the do-nothing operation differ by the sign of a determinant, the sign takes only two values, and no continuous path of transformations gets from one to the other without leaving the set of allowed transformations. There is no dial to turn, so there is no derivative at zero, no generator, and no conserved current.

What such a symmetry offers instead exists only once states can carry labels, and it is a multiplicative label, usually plus or minus one, whose product over everything present is the same before a reaction as after. Additive quantities come from symmetries you can apply by degrees and multiplicative ones from symmetries you cannot, and they are different objects obeying different arithmetic.

Nature turns out to violate two of the three, which was a genuine surprise, since nothing in mechanics or electromagnetism gives any reason for the laws to distinguish left from right. Nothing quietly breaks when they fail, because there was no charge to lose and no continuity equation to spoil; the symmetry is merely absent. The one combination that does appear to survive is not luck but a theorem, forced by requirements the later parts of this book impose.

6 · Fields: symmetry gives a conserved current

Chapter 1.2 §8 showed that the Euler–Lagrange derivation goes through verbatim for fields, with one substitution: replace L(q,q˙,t)L(q,\dot q,t)L(q,q˙​,t) by a Lagrangian density L(ϕ,∂μϕ)\mathcal{L}(\phi,\partial_{\mu}\phi)L(ϕ,∂μ​ϕ), replace ∫dt\int\dd t∫dt by ∫d4x\int\dd^{4}x∫d4x, and replace ddt\dv{}{t}dtd​ by ∂μ\partial_{\mu}∂μ​. The same substitution turns §2 into the field version of Noether's theorem, and the result is more useful than the mechanics version.

Take an internal symmetry — one that transforms the field at each point without moving the point:

δϕ  =  ϵ K(ϕ),δ(∂μϕ)  =  ∂μ(δϕ),δL  =  ϵ ∂μFμ. \delta\phi \;=\; \epsilon\,K(\phi), \qquad \delta\big(\partial_{\mu}\phi\big) \;=\; \partial_{\mu}\big(\delta\phi\big), \qquad \delta\mathcal{L} \;=\; \epsilon\,\partial_{\mu}F^{\mu}. δϕ=ϵK(ϕ),δ(∂μ​ϕ)=∂μ​(δϕ),δL=ϵ∂μ​Fμ. (1.4.32)

The middle equation is Step 1 again — variations commute with derivatives — and the right-hand one is the symmetry hypothesis, with the total time derivative promoted to a four-divergence, since that is now what integrates to a boundary term. Steps 2 and 3 are unchanged. Expand by the chain rule, then use the field Euler–Lagrange equation ∂μ(∂L/∂(∂μϕ))=∂L/∂ϕ\partial_{\mu}\big(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial(\partial_{\mu}\phi)\big)=\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\phi∂μ​(∂L/∂(∂μ​ϕ))=∂L/∂ϕ:

δL=∂L∂ϕ δϕ+∂L∂(∂μϕ) ∂μ(δϕ)=ϵ[∂μ ⁣(∂L∂(∂μϕ))K+∂L∂(∂μϕ) ∂μK]  =  ϵ ∂μ ⁣[∂L∂(∂μϕ) K]. \begin{aligned} \delta\mathcal{L} &= \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{\phi}\,\delta\phi + \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)}\,\partial_{\mu}\big(\delta\phi\big)\\[4pt] &= \epsilon\left[\partial_{\mu}\!\left(\pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)}\right)K + \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)}\,\partial_{\mu}K\right] \;=\; \epsilon\,\partial_{\mu}\!\left[\pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)}\,K\right]. \end{aligned} δL​=∂ϕ∂L​δϕ+∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​∂μ​(δϕ)=ϵ[∂μ​(∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​)K+∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​∂μ​K]=ϵ∂μ​[∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​K].​ (1.4.33)

Compare with the hypothesis and the four-divergence of the difference vanishes:

  jμ  =  ∂L∂(∂μϕ) K  −  Fμ,∂μjμ  =  0.   \boxed{\;j^{\mu} \;=\; \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)}\,K \;-\; F^{\mu}, \qquad \partial_{\mu}j^{\mu} \;=\; 0.\;} jμ=∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​K−Fμ,∂μ​jμ=0.​ (1.4.34)

6.1 · This is the continuity equation, and that is a promotion

Split jμ=(j0,j)j^{\mu}=(j^{0},\vv j)jμ=(j0,j) into its time and space parts. Then ∂μjμ=∂tj0+∇⋅j\partial_{\mu}j^{\mu}=\partial_{t}j^{0}+\nabla\cdot\vv j∂μ​jμ=∂t​j0+∇⋅j, and (1.4.34) is

∂j0∂t  +  ∇⋅j  =  0, \pdv{j^{0}}{t} \;+\; \nabla\cdot\vv j \;=\; 0, ∂t∂j0​+∇⋅j=0, (1.4.35)

which is precisely the continuity equation of Chapter 0.7, with j0j^{0}j0 the density of the conserved stuff and j\vv jj its current. Chapter 0.7 promised that Noether's theorem would deliver one of these; here it is. Integrating over a region VVV and applying the divergence theorem, exactly as in that chapter,

Q  =  ∫Vj0 d3x⟹dQdt  =  −∮∂Vj⋅dA. Q \;=\; \int_{V} j^{0}\,\dd^{3}x \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dv{Q}{t} \;=\; -\oint_{\partial V}\vv j\cdot\dd\vv A. Q=∫V​j0d3x⟹dtdQ​=−∮∂V​j⋅dA. (1.4.36)

Now notice how much stronger this is than the mechanics version. In §2 we proved that a number Q(t)Q(t)Q(t) does not change. Here we have proved something local: the charge in any region changes only by flux through that region's boundary. Charge cannot vanish in London and reappear in Sydney with the books still balancing — to get from one to the other it must cross every surface in between. Field conservation laws forbid teleportation; mechanical ones do not. That is not a stylistic upgrade. It is the difference between a conservation law compatible with special relativity and one that is not, since a global bookkeeping rule requires a notion of "at the same instant everywhere" that Chapter 2.2 will destroy.

Grind box — the current is not unique, and the ambiguity is useful

Suppose jμj^{\mu}jμ is conserved and let Σνμ\Sigma^{\nu\mu}Σνμ be any field antisymmetric in its two indices, Σνμ=−Σμν\Sigma^{\nu\mu}=-\Sigma^{\mu\nu}Σνμ=−Σμν. Define

j~μ  =  jμ+∂νΣνμ. \tilde j^{\mu} \;=\; j^{\mu} + \partial_{\nu}\Sigma^{\nu\mu}. j~​μ=jμ+∂ν​Σνμ.

Then ∂μj~μ=∂μjμ+∂μ∂νΣνμ=0\partial_{\mu}\tilde j^{\mu} = \partial_{\mu}j^{\mu} + \partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}\Sigma^{\nu\mu} = 0∂μ​j~​μ=∂μ​jμ+∂μ​∂ν​Σνμ=0, because ∂μ∂ν\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}∂μ​∂ν​ is symmetric in μν\mu\nuμν (equality of mixed partials, Chapter 0.6) while Σνμ\Sigma^{\nu\mu}Σνμ is antisymmetric, and a symmetric object fully contracted with an antisymmetric one vanishes — the identical argument used in §3.3's grind box. The new current is conserved too.

Does it carry the same charge? The added piece contributes ∫∂νΣν0d3x\int\partial_{\nu}\Sigma^{\nu0}\dd^{3}x∫∂ν​Σν0d3x. The ν=0\nu=0ν=0 term vanishes by antisymmetry (Σ00=0\Sigma^{00}=0Σ00=0), leaving ∫∂iΣi0d3x\int\partial_{i}\Sigma^{i0}\dd^{3}x∫∂i​Σi0d3x, a total spatial divergence, which by the divergence theorem is a surface integral at infinity. If the fields fall off, it is zero and Q~=Q\tilde Q = QQ~​=Q. So the current is ambiguous but the charge is not.

This is not idle. The Noether procedure applied to spacetime translations produces an energy–momentum tensor TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν that is in general not symmetric in its indices, which is a disaster for general relativity, where TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν sits on the right-hand side of a manifestly symmetric field equation (Chapter 3.6). The repair is exactly this freedom: one adds a suitable ∂νΣνμρ\partial_{\nu}\Sigma^{\nu\mu\rho}∂ν​Σνμρ — an "improvement term" — to symmetrise TμνT^{\mu\nu}Tμν without changing a single conserved charge. Chapter 5.2 does it.

6.2 · The example that sets up Part VI: a global phase

Take a complex scalar field ϕ\phiϕ, with ϕ\phiϕ and its conjugate ϕ∗\phi^{*}ϕ∗ treated as independent (which is legitimate for the same reason xxx and x˙\dot xx˙ were in Chapter 1.2 — they are independent slots of the function, and any complex ϕ\phiϕ can be traded for the real pair (Re⁡ϕ,Im⁡ϕ)(\operatorname{Re}\phi,\operatorname{Im}\phi)(Reϕ,Imϕ) and back):

L  =  ∂μϕ∗ ∂μϕ  −  m2ϕ∗ϕ. \mathcal{L} \;=\; \partial_{\mu}\phi^{*}\,\partial^{\mu}\phi \;-\; m^{2}\phi^{*}\phi. L=∂μ​ϕ∗∂μϕ−m2ϕ∗ϕ. (1.4.37)

Now rotate the phase of the field by the same angle everywhere:

ϕ  ⟼  eiαϕ,ϕ∗  ⟼  e−iαϕ∗,α a real constant. \phi \;\longmapsto\; \ee^{\ii\alpha}\phi, \qquad \phi^{*} \;\longmapsto\; \ee^{-\ii\alpha}\phi^{*}, \qquad \alpha \text{ a real constant}. ϕ⟼eiαϕ,ϕ∗⟼e−iαϕ∗,α a real constant. (1.4.38)

Every term in (1.4.37) pairs a ϕ\phiϕ with a ϕ∗\phi^{*}ϕ∗, so the phases cancel exactly: L\mathcal{L}L is strictly invariant, Fμ=0F^{\mu}=0Fμ=0. This is a global U(1)U(1)U(1) symmetry — U(1)U(1)U(1) because the transformations are the unit complex numbers eiα\ee^{\ii\alpha}eiα, which form a circle group under multiplication, and global because α\alphaα is the same at every point of spacetime.

Infinitesimally, ϵ=α\epsilon=\alphaϵ=α and Kϕ=iϕK_{\phi}=\ii\phiKϕ​=iϕ, Kϕ∗=−iϕ∗K_{\phi^{*}}=-\ii\phi^{*}Kϕ∗​=−iϕ∗. The two derivatives needed are ∂L/∂(∂μϕ)=∂μϕ∗\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial(\partial_{\mu}\phi)=\partial^{\mu}\phi^{*}∂L/∂(∂μ​ϕ)=∂μϕ∗ and ∂L/∂(∂μϕ∗)=∂μϕ\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial(\partial_{\mu}\phi^{*})=\partial^{\mu}\phi∂L/∂(∂μ​ϕ∗)=∂μϕ, so (1.4.34) summed over both fields gives

jμ  =  i(ϕ ∂μϕ∗  −  ϕ∗∂μϕ). j^{\mu} \;=\; \ii\Big(\phi\,\partial^{\mu}\phi^{*} \;-\; \phi^{*}\partial^{\mu}\phi\Big). jμ=i(ϕ∂μϕ∗−ϕ∗∂μϕ). (1.4.39)

Two checks. It is real: complex-conjugating swaps the two terms and the i\iii out front, giving back the same expression. And it is conserved directly, without invoking the theorem — take the divergence, note that the terms with two derivatives on different factors cancel in pairs, and use the field equation □ϕ=−m2ϕ\Box\phi=-m^{2}\phi□ϕ=−m2ϕ from (1.4.37):

∂μjμ  =  i(ϕ □ϕ∗−ϕ∗□ϕ)  =  i(−m2ϕϕ∗+m2ϕ∗ϕ)  =  0. \partial_{\mu}j^{\mu} \;=\; \ii\Big(\phi\,\Box\phi^{*} - \phi^{*}\Box\phi\Big) \;=\; \ii\Big(-m^{2}\phi\phi^{*} + m^{2}\phi^{*}\phi\Big) \;=\; 0. ∂μ​jμ=i(ϕ□ϕ∗−ϕ∗□ϕ)=i(−m2ϕϕ∗+m2ϕ∗ϕ)=0. (1.4.40)

Multiplying a conserved current by any constant leaves it conserved, so the normalisation and overall sign are conventions; fixing them by the requirement that a positive-energy mode carry positive charge, the physical electromagnetic current of a field of charge qqq is −q jμ-q\,j^{\mu}−qjμ. The conserved quantity Q=∫j0d3xQ=\int j^{0}\dd^{3}xQ=∫j0d3x is, up to that constant, electric charge.

The question you should be holding

The symmetry above required α\alphaα to be the same everywhere. That is a peculiar demand. It says that if you rotate the phase of the field in this room you must simultaneously rotate it, by exactly the same angle, in a galaxy ten billion light-years away — and Chapter 2.2 is about to make "simultaneously" a suspect word. A relativist's instinct is that a symmetry requiring instantaneous agreement across the universe is not a symmetry that should be taken seriously in that form.

So: what happens if you insist that α\alphaα may depend on position, α→α(x)\alpha\to\alpha(x)α→α(x)?

The answer is that (1.4.37) is no longer invariant — the derivative ∂μ\partial_{\mu}∂μ​ hits α(x)\alpha(x)α(x) and leaves a term behind — and the only way to repair it is to introduce a new field whose transformation law is designed to cancel that term. The new field turns out to be the electromagnetic potential AμA_{\mu}Aμ​, and its dynamics turn out to be Maxwell's equations. Demanding that a global symmetry be made local is called the gauge principle, and it does not merely accommodate electromagnetism — it generates it, and with a bigger group it generates the strong and weak forces as well. That is Chapter 6.3, and it is the single largest cheque this book writes. Nothing more will be said about it here; the point is only that you now know exactly which question leads there.

⚑ One warning to file, since it explains why Chapter 6.3 cannot simply run §6 again. Noether proved two theorems in 1918. The first is the one above, for symmetries with finitely many parameters. The second concerns symmetries depending on arbitrary functions — gauge symmetries — and its conclusion is different in kind: instead of conserved charges it yields identities among the equations of motion, which is why gauge theories have constraints, why the Bianchi identity of Chapter 3.4 exists, and why ∇μTμν=0\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}=0∇μ​Tμν=0 is automatic in general relativity rather than imposed.

Familiar ground — the indicator-dilution equation is a conservation law

You have taken a cardiac output off an indicator-dilution curve. Inject a known mass mmm of dye or a known thermal deficit upstream, sample downstream, and

Q  =  m∫0∞c(t) dt, Q \;=\; \frac{m}{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty} c(t)\,\dd t}, Q=∫0∞​c(t)dtm​,

which is the Stewart–Hamilton equation. It is (1.4.36) with a different name on the conserved stuff, and its derivation is the one just given.

Take the conserved density to be the indicator concentration, j0=cj^{0}=cj0=c, and the current to be j=c v\vv j = c\,\vv vj=cv. Indestructibility of the indicator is exactly (1.4.35). Now integrate over the vascular volume lying between the injection site and the sampling site. Immediately after the injection that region holds all of mmm; long afterwards it holds none; and the only boundary through which anything leaves is the sampling plane. So (1.4.36), integrated over all time, reads ∫0∞ ⁣∮∂Vj⋅dA  dt=m\int_{0}^{\infty}\!\oint_{\partial V}\vv j\cdot\dd\vv A\;\dd t = m∫0∞​∮∂V​j⋅dAdt=m, and with flow QQQ across a plane of uniform concentration the flux is Q c(t)Q\,c(t)Qc(t). Hence Q∫c dt=mQ\int c\,\dd t = mQ∫cdt=m. That is the whole derivation.

The local statement is the one doing the work. A purely global rule — "all the dye that goes in comes out eventually" — is perfectly compatible with dye vanishing at the injection site and reappearing at the catheter tip, and under that hypothesis the area under the curve tells you nothing whatever about a flow. It is §6.1's stronger claim, that the amount inside any region changes only by crossing that region's boundary, which turns an area under a curve into millilitres per minute. Both standard corrections to the method are repairs to a violated conservation law rather than to the arithmetic: recirculation means indicator crosses the sampling plane twice, so the integral double-counts and QQQ comes out too low, which is why the downslope is fitted with an exponential and extrapolated; thermal loss to the catheter and the vessel wall is a genuine sink term on the right of (1.4.35), removing indicator without transporting it, and QQQ comes out too high.

Where the correspondence stops, and it stops sharply. Noether's theorem does not supply this conservation law. Nobody derives the indestructibility of indocyanine green from an invariance of an action; it is assumed, and the assumption is precisely what those two corrections are defending. What §6 delivers is the arrow running the other way — hand it a symmetry and a conserved current appears whether or not anyone was expecting one, together with an explicit formula (1.4.34) for what the conserved stuff is. That is a stronger kind of statement than a mass balance, and §6.2 spends it on a quantity nobody would have guessed.

In plain terms 1.4.6

Repeating the proof with a field in place of a coordinate costs nothing and returns much more. The same steps, with a four-dimensional divergence in place of a time derivative, deliver not a number that fails to change but a density and a current, tied by the statement that the density's rate of increase at a point equals what flows out. That is the equation promised when local conservation was first set out.

The gain deserves stating exactly. A global law says a grand total, added over everything, is the same at one moment as another. A local law says the amount inside any region changes only by crossing its boundary, so nothing may leave one place and arrive at another without traversing the ground between. The difference is not stylistic: a global ledger needs a notion of the same moment everywhere, and the next part of this book dismantles it.

The example to keep is a field of complex values whose scalar is unchanged when the phase is turned by one angle everywhere, and whose conserved quantity is, up to a constant, electric charge. That the angle must be the same everywhere should look suspicious for the reason already given, demanding as it does instantaneous agreement across the universe. Asking what happens when the angle may vary from place to place is the question that produces every force in nature.

7 · The other direction: charges generate their own symmetries

So far the arrow runs one way: symmetry ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ conserved charge. This section runs it backwards, and the result is the real destination of Part I.

Chapter 1.3 supplies the tool. On phase space, coordinates qiq_{i}qi​ and momenta pip_{i}pi​ are independent, and any two functions of them have a Poisson bracket

{f,g}  =  ∑i(∂f∂qi∂g∂pi−∂f∂pi∂g∂qi), \{f,g\} \;=\; \sum_{i}\left(\pdv{f}{q_{i}}\pdv{g}{p_{i}} - \pdv{f}{p_{i}}\pdv{g}{q_{i}}\right), {f,g}=i∑​(∂qi​∂f​∂pi​∂g​−∂pi​∂f​∂qi​∂g​), (1.4.41)

with the two facts we need: time evolution is dfdt={f,H}+∂f/∂t\dv{f}{t}=\{f,H\}+\partial f/\partial tdtdf​={f,H}+∂f/∂t, and a function GGG generates an infinitesimal transformation of phase space through

δf  =  ϵ {f,G}. \delta f \;=\; \epsilon\,\{f,G\}. δf=ϵ{f,G}. (1.4.42)

7.1 · The charge is the generator — in one line

Take a Noether charge of the standard form (1.4.15) with τ=0\tau=0τ=0, namely Q=∑ipiKi(q,t)−F(q,t)Q=\sum_{i}p_{i}K_{i}(q,t)-F(q,t)Q=∑i​pi​Ki​(q,t)−F(q,t), and ask what transformation it generates. Only the first term contains any ppp, and it is linear in them — which is exactly where the restriction to Ki(q,t)K_{i}(q,t)Ki​(q,t) is spent. §1.1 allowed Ki(q,q˙,t)K_{i}(q,\dot q,t)Ki​(q,q˙​,t); a velocity-dependent generator makes QQQ quadratic in the momenta and the bracket below returns something else. So, for generators of the narrower kind,

δqj  =  ϵ {qj,Q}  =  ϵ ∂Q∂pj  =  ϵ Kj. \delta q_{j} \;=\; \epsilon\,\{q_{j},Q\} \;=\; \epsilon\,\pdv{Q}{p_{j}} \;=\; \epsilon\,K_{j}. δqj​=ϵ{qj​,Q}=ϵ∂pj​∂Q​=ϵKj​. (1.4.43)

That is not an analogy or a coincidence: it is an identity, and it says that the Noether charge of a symmetry, used as a generator, reproduces exactly the symmetry it came from. The theorem and its converse are the same equation read in opposite directions. Three instances, worth doing explicitly because the brackets are how you will compute in Part IV.

Momentum generates translations. With G=pxG=p_{x}G=px​, equation (1.4.41) gives {x,px}=1\{x,p_{x}\}=1{x,px​}=1 and {y,px}={pi,px}=0\{y,p_{x}\}=\{p_{i},p_{x}\}=0{y,px​}={pi​,px​}=0, so

δx=ϵ,δy=δz=0,δp=0. \delta x = \epsilon, \qquad \delta y = \delta z = 0, \qquad \delta\vv p = 0. δx=ϵ,δy=δz=0,δp=0. (1.4.44)

A rigid translation along xxx, exactly as advertised.

Angular momentum generates rotations. With G=Lz=xpy−ypxG=L_{z}=xp_{y}-yp_{x}G=Lz​=xpy​−ypx​, the derivatives are ∂Lz/∂px=−y\partial L_{z}/\partial p_{x}=-y∂Lz​/∂px​=−y, ∂Lz/∂py=x\partial L_{z}/\partial p_{y}=x∂Lz​/∂py​=x, ∂Lz/∂x=py\partial L_{z}/\partial x=p_{y}∂Lz​/∂x=py​, ∂Lz/∂y=−px\partial L_{z}/\partial y=-p_{x}∂Lz​/∂y=−px​, so

δx=ϵ{x,Lz}=−ϵy,δy=ϵ{y,Lz}=+ϵx,δpx=ϵ{px,Lz}=−ϵpy,δpy=ϵ{py,Lz}=+ϵpx. \begin{aligned} \delta x &= \epsilon\{x,L_{z}\} = -\epsilon y, & \delta y &= \epsilon\{y,L_{z}\} = +\epsilon x,\\[3pt] \delta p_{x} &= \epsilon\{p_{x},L_{z}\} = -\epsilon p_{y}, & \delta p_{y} &= \epsilon\{p_{y},L_{z}\} = +\epsilon p_{x}. \end{aligned} δxδpx​​=ϵ{x,Lz​}=−ϵy,=ϵ{px​,Lz​}=−ϵpy​,​δyδpy​​=ϵ{y,Lz​}=+ϵx,=ϵ{py​,Lz​}=+ϵpx​.​ (1.4.45)

The position rotates by ϵ\epsilonϵ about the zzz-axis, and — a bonus the Lagrangian derivation never showed us — so does the momentum, which is exactly right, since momentum is a vector and vectors rotate.

The Hamiltonian generates time evolution. With G=HG=HG=H, equation (1.4.42) reads δf=ϵ{f,H}=ϵ dfdt\delta f=\epsilon\{f,H\}=\epsilon\,\dv{f}{t}δf=ϵ{f,H}=ϵdtdf​ for any fff without explicit time dependence, which is the statement that the transformation generated by HHH is advance everything by ϵ\epsilonϵ. Time evolution is not a different kind of process from a symmetry transformation; it is the symmetry transformation generated by the energy. (And this is where the minus sign in (1.4.15) pays: the Noether charge of time translation is −H-H−H, which generates δf=−ϵdfdt\delta f=-\epsilon\dv{f}{t}δf=−ϵdtdf​ — the shift of the graph of q(t)q(t)q(t) forward by ϵ\epsilonϵ, which at fixed ttt shows you the value the old path had at t−ϵt-\epsilont−ϵ. The two signs describe the same motion from opposite sides.)

7.2 · The converse, and why it is not decorative

Now the reverse implication. Suppose QQQ is conserved and has no explicit time dependence. Then 0=dQdt={Q,H}0=\dv{Q}{t}=\{Q,H\}0=dtdQ​={Q,H}, and therefore the transformation QQQ generates does this to the Hamiltonian:

δH  =  ϵ {H,Q}  =  −ϵ {Q,H}  =  0. \delta H \;=\; \epsilon\,\{H,Q\} \;=\; -\epsilon\,\{Q,H\} \;=\; 0. δH=ϵ{H,Q}=−ϵ{Q,H}=0. (1.4.46)

The Hamiltonian is invariant under the transformation generated by QQQ. So QQQ is not merely produced by a symmetry; QQQ is a symmetry, viewed as a generator. There is nothing left to prove in either direction.

The destination of Part I

Symmetries and conservation laws are not cause and effect. They are the same object, viewed twice. Given a symmetry, (1.4.15) hands you a function on phase space. Given that function, (1.4.42) hands you back the symmetry. The Noether charge and the generator are one thing wearing two names, and which name you use depends only on whether you are asking "what stays the same?" or "what moves?"

This has structural consequences that outrun mechanics. The charges close under the bracket: §3.3's grind box promised, and §7.3 verifies, that {Li,Lj}=εijkLk\{L_{i},L_{j}\}=\varepsilon_{ijk}L_{k}{Li​,Lj​}=εijk​Lk​ — the bracket of two conserved charges is again a conserved charge, with coefficients fixed by how the symmetries themselves compose. That structure is a Lie algebra, and it is the algebra of the symmetry group. Chapter 6.1 studies it systematically; Chapter 4.7 finds the identical relation with commutators in place of brackets, [L^i,L^j]=iℏεijkL^k[\hat L_{i},\hat L_{j}]=\ii\hbar\varepsilon_{ijk}\hat L_{k}[L^i​,L^j​]=iℏεijk​L^k​, and derives the entire quantum theory of angular momentum — including half-integer spin, which has no classical counterpart — from nothing but that algebra.

This is what licenses the sentence this book keeps repeating. Pick a symmetry, write the most general action invariant under it, quantise. Step one is now a precise instruction: name a Lie group. Step two is Chapter 1.2. Step three replaces { ,}\{\,,\}{,} by 1iℏ[ ,]\tfrac{1}{\ii\hbar}[\,,]iℏ1​[,] and is Chapter 5.3. Every remaining part of this book is that recipe with a different group in step one.

7.3 · The algebra of the rotation charges

Grind box — computing {Li,Lj}\{L_{i},L_{j}\}{Li​,Lj​} by hand

Take Lx=ypz−zpyL_{x}=yp_{z}-zp_{y}Lx​=ypz​−zpy​ and Ly=zpx−xpzL_{y}=zp_{x}-xp_{z}Ly​=zpx​−xpz​ and grind (1.4.41) over the three coordinate pairs. Only terms in which the same variable is differentiated in both factors survive. The nonzero partials are

∂Lx∂y=pz,∂Lx∂z=−py,∂Lx∂py=−z,∂Lx∂pz=y,∂Ly∂z=px,∂Ly∂x=−pz,∂Ly∂pz=−x,∂Ly∂px=z. \begin{aligned} &\pdv{L_{x}}{y}=p_{z}, && \pdv{L_{x}}{z}=-p_{y}, && \pdv{L_{x}}{p_{y}}=-z, && \pdv{L_{x}}{p_{z}}=y,\\[3pt] &\pdv{L_{y}}{z}=p_{x}, && \pdv{L_{y}}{x}=-p_{z}, && \pdv{L_{y}}{p_{z}}=-x, && \pdv{L_{y}}{p_{x}}=z. \end{aligned} ​∂y∂Lx​​=pz​,∂z∂Ly​​=px​,​​∂z∂Lx​​=−py​,∂x∂Ly​​=−pz​,​​∂py​∂Lx​​=−z,∂pz​∂Ly​​=−x,​​∂pz​∂Lx​​=y,∂px​∂Ly​​=z.​

Assemble the bracket term by term. From the xxx-pair: ∂xLx ∂pxLy−∂pxLx ∂xLy=0⋅z−0⋅(−pz)=0\partial_{x}L_{x}\,\partial_{p_{x}}L_{y}-\partial_{p_{x}}L_{x}\,\partial_{x}L_{y} = 0\cdot z - 0\cdot(-p_{z}) = 0∂x​Lx​∂px​​Ly​−∂px​​Lx​∂x​Ly​=0⋅z−0⋅(−pz​)=0. From the yyy-pair: pz⋅0−(−z)(0)=0p_{z}\cdot 0 - (-z)(0) = 0pz​⋅0−(−z)(0)=0. From the zzz-pair: (−py)(−x)−(y)(px)=xpy−ypx(-p_{y})(-x) - (y)(p_{x}) = xp_{y}-yp_{x}(−py​)(−x)−(y)(px​)=xpy​−ypx​. Hence

{Lx,Ly}  =  xpy−ypx  =  Lz, \{L_{x},L_{y}\} \;=\; xp_{y}-yp_{x} \;=\; L_{z}, {Lx​,Ly​}=xpy​−ypx​=Lz​,

and by relabelling x→y→z→xx\to y\to z\to xx→y→z→x, which permutes the three definitions cyclically,

{Li,Lj}  =  εijkLk. \{L_{i},L_{j}\} \;=\; \varepsilon_{ijk}L_{k}. {Li​,Lj​}=εijk​Lk​.

(Verified symbolically for all nine pairs.) Two remarks. First, the right-hand side is not zero, and that non-vanishing is the algebraic residue of the geometric fact that rotations about different axes do not commute — the bracket of generators measures the failure of the transformations to commute. Second, the same computation for translations gives {Pi,Pj}=0\{P_{i},P_{j}\}=0{Pi​,Pj​}=0, because translations do commute. The bracket is a faithful record of the group.

One consequence you can already read off, and which Chapter 4.7 turns into the whole theory of spin: since {Lx,Ly}≠0\{L_{x},L_{y}\}\neq0{Lx​,Ly​}=0, the three components of angular momentum are not simultaneously "diagonalisable" in the sense that will matter after quantisation. You will be able to know ∣L∣\abs{\vv L}∣L∣ and one component, and no more.

⚠ Why this isn't obvious

A symmetry of the equations of motion is not the same thing as a symmetry of the action, and only the second kind gives a Noether charge. This is the second hypothesis that popular statements of the theorem drop.

Take the free particle, L=12mx˙2L=\half m\dot x^{2}L=21​mx˙2, whose equation of motion is mx¨=0m\ddot x=0mx¨=0. Now scale the coordinate, x↦(1+ϵ)xx\mapsto(1+\epsilon)xx↦(1+ϵ)x, leaving ttt alone. The equation of motion is completely unbothered: it is linear and homogeneous, so if x(t)x(t)x(t) is a solution then so is any multiple of it. Every solution maps to a solution. Yet the action is not invariant —

L  ⟼  12m(1+ϵ)2x˙2  =  L+2ϵL+O(ϵ2), L \;\longmapsto\; \half m(1+\epsilon)^{2}\dot x^{2} \;=\; L + 2\epsilon L + O(\epsilon^{2}), L⟼21​m(1+ϵ)2x˙2=L+2ϵL+O(ϵ2),

so δL=2ϵL\delta L = 2\epsilon LδL=2ϵL, which is not a total time derivative for a general path (if it were, LLL would contribute nothing to the equations of motion, and it plainly does). So this is not a symmetry in the sense of §1.2, and the theorem does not apply.

Test the conclusion rather than trusting it. If the theorem did apply, the generator is K=xK=xK=x and the charge would be Q=px=mxx˙Q=px=m x\dot xQ=px=mxx˙. Differentiate along a solution: dQdt=mx˙2+mxx¨=mx˙2≠0\dv{Q}{t} = m\dot x^{2}+mx\ddot x = m\dot x^{2} \neq 0dtdQ​=mx˙2+mxx¨=mx˙2=0. Not conserved. The theorem was right to refuse.

What such a transformation gives instead is a map from solutions to other solutions — useful information, but of a different type. Problem 4 develops the most famous example: the scaling that maps Kepler orbits to other Kepler orbits, which is not a symmetry of the action, has no conserved charge, and is nevertheless the origin of Kepler's third law.

In plain terms 1.4.7

The last step reverses the arrow, and shows there was never an arrow to reverse. Take the conserved quantity a symmetry produced, feed it back as a generator of motion, and what it generates is the symmetry it came from. Not an analogy but an identity. A conserved quantity and a symmetry are one object under two names, and which you reach for depends on whether you ask what stays the same or what moves.

These quantities close among themselves: combining two returns a third, with coefficients fixed by how the transformations compose. Rotations about different axes do not commute and their combination is not zero; translations do commute and theirs is. That structure is what a symmetry group concretely amounts to, and it makes the book's recurring instruction precise: name a group, write the most general scalar invariant under it, quantise.

Part I is finished. Forces are gone, replaced by one number attached to each history, nature selecting the one where that number stops changing; a single point now fixes a whole future; and every continuous symmetry hands over a conserved quantity that is the symmetry itself. One thing was left broken, when the momentum of two moving charges refused to add up. Repairing it means surrendering something so ordinary nobody has troubled to state it, that everybody shares one clock; the next part opens on the collision between electromagnetism and that assumption.

8 · Worked examples

Worked example 1 — the Galilean boost, and a conservation law nobody names

§1.3 established that the boost (1.4.5) is a symmetry of the NNN-body Lagrangian (1.4.4), but only in the loosened sense: it changes LLL by the total derivative of F=Mu⋅RcmF=M\vv u\cdot\vv R_{\rm cm}F=Mu⋅Rcm​. Now collect the charge. The ingredients are

Ka=u t,τ=0,F=u⋅∑amaxa, \vv K_{a} = \vv u\,t, \qquad \tau = 0, \qquad F = \vv u\cdot\sum_{a}m_{a}\vv x_{a}, Ka​=ut,τ=0,F=u⋅a∑​ma​xa​,

and (1.4.15) gives

Q=∑apa⋅(u t)−u⋅∑amaxa=u⋅(P t−MRcm). Q = \sum_{a}\vv p_{a}\cdot\big(\vv u\,t\big) - \vv u\cdot\sum_{a}m_{a}\vv x_{a} = \vv u\cdot\Big(\vv P\,t - M\vv R_{\rm cm}\Big). Q=a∑​pa​⋅(ut)−u⋅a∑​ma​xa​=u⋅(Pt−MRcm​).

Since u\vv uu was an arbitrary boost direction, all three components are conserved:

  N  =  P t  −  MRcm  =  constant.   \boxed{\;\vv N \;=\; \vv P\,t \;-\; M\vv R_{\rm cm} \;=\; \text{constant.}\;} N=Pt−MRcm​=constant.​

Check it directly. dNdt=P+t dPdt−MR˙cm\dv{\vv N}{t} = \vv P + t\,\dv{\vv P}{t} - M\dot{\vv R}_{\rm cm}dtdN​=P+tdtdP​−MR˙cm​. The middle term vanishes because P\vv PP is conserved (§3.2 — the same potential-depends-on- differences hypothesis), and MR˙cm=∑amax˙a=PM\dot{\vv R}_{\rm cm}=\sum_{a}m_{a}\dot{\vv x}_{a}=\vv PMR˙cm​=∑a​ma​x˙a​=P by definition. So dNdt=P−P=0\dv{\vv N}{t}=\vv P-\vv P=0dtdN​=P−P=0. ✓

What it says. Rearrange:

Rcm(t)  =  PM t  −  NM. \vv R_{\rm cm}(t) \;=\; \frac{\vv P}{M}\,t \;-\; \frac{\vv N}{M}. Rcm​(t)=MP​t−MN​.

The centre of mass moves in a straight line at constant velocity, forever, whatever the particles inside are doing to each other. That is a statement everybody knows and almost nobody files under "conservation law", because the conserved quantity has no name and no symbol in the standard curriculum. It has one here: it is the Noether charge of the boost, and it sits in the table of §3.4 alongside energy and momentum with exactly the same status.

Two things worth noticing. First, N\vv NN depends explicitly on ttt. Nothing in the theorem forbade that — KKK was allowed to depend on ttt, and here K=ut\vv K=\vv u tK=ut does. A conserved quantity need not be a function of the instantaneous state alone; it is a combination of the state and the clock that happens to be constant. Second, this is the charge that has no analogue after Chapter 2. The Galilean group's boosts get replaced by Lorentz boosts, whose Noether charges are the components of a relativistic object (Chapter 2.5) with a rather different physical reading. The centre-of-mass theorem is a specifically Newtonian statement, and it is a good illustration of the general rule that changing the symmetry group changes the list of conserved quantities, which is the whole reason the rest of this book is organised by symmetry group.

Worked example 2 — the Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector, and a hidden symmetry

Take the Kepler problem: one particle of mass mmm in the attractive potential

V(r)=−kr,so thatp˙=−kr2 r^,r^=rr. V(r) = -\frac{k}{r}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad \dot{\vv p} = -\frac{k}{r^{2}}\,\hat{\vv r}, \qquad \hat{\vv r} = \frac{\vv r}{r}. V(r)=−rk​,so thatp˙​=−r2k​r^,r^=rr​.

Rotational symmetry gives L=r×p\vv L=\vv r\times\vv pL=r×p conserved (§3.3), and time-translation symmetry gives EEE conserved (§3.1). That is four constants; a generic central force gives no more. But the 1/r1/r1/r potential has a fifth, discovered and rediscovered so often it carries three names:

  A  =  p×L  −  mk r^   \boxed{\;\vv A \;=\; \vv p\times\vv L \;-\; mk\,\hat{\vv r}\;} A=p×L−mkr^​

It is conserved, and the proof is three lines of vector algebra done in the grind box below. The key move is that the awkward-looking r^×(r×r˙)\hat{\vv r}\times(\vv r\times\dot{\vv r})r^×(r×r˙) collapses, by the a×(b×c)\vv a\times(\vv b\times\vv c)a×(b×c) expansion, into exactly r2ddt(r/r)r^{2}\dv{}{t}(\vv r/r)r2dtd​(r/r) — so the rate of change of p×L\vv p\times\vv Lp×L is mk dr^dtmk\,\dv{\hat{\vv r}}{t}mkdtdr^​, and subtracting mkr^mk\hat{\vv r}mkr^ cancels it.

Grind box — proving dAdt=0\dv{\vv A}{t}=0dtdA​=0, and two identities that come free

Conservation. L\vv LL is constant (§3.3), so only the first factor moves:

ddt(p×L)=p˙×L=−kr2 r^×(m r×r˙). \dv{}{t}\big(\vv p\times\vv L\big) = \dot{\vv p}\times\vv L = -\frac{k}{r^{2}}\,\hat{\vv r}\times\big(m\,\vv r\times\dot{\vv r}\big). dtd​(p×L)=p˙​×L=−r2k​r^×(mr×r˙).

Apply a×(b×c)=b(a⋅c)−c(a⋅b)\vv a\times(\vv b\times\vv c)=\vv b(\vv a\cdot\vv c)-\vv c(\vv a\cdot\vv b)a×(b×c)=b(a⋅c)−c(a⋅b) with a=r^\vv a=\hat{\vv r}a=r^, b=r\vv b=\vv rb=r, c=r˙\vv c=\dot{\vv r}c=r˙, and use r^⋅r˙=r˙\hat{\vv r}\cdot\dot{\vv r}=\dot rr^⋅r˙=r˙ together with r^⋅r=r\hat{\vv r}\cdot\vv r=rr^⋅r=r:

p˙×L=−mkr2[r r˙−r˙ r]=mk[r˙r−r r˙r2]=mk ddt ⁣(rr)=mk dr^dt, \begin{aligned} \dot{\vv p}\times\vv L &= -\frac{mk}{r^{2}}\Big[\vv r\,\dot r - \dot{\vv r}\,r\Big] = mk\left[\frac{\dot{\vv r}}{r} - \frac{\vv r\,\dot r}{r^{2}}\right]\\[4pt] &= mk\,\dv{}{t}\!\left(\frac{\vv r}{r}\right) = mk\,\dv{\hat{\vv r}}{t}, \end{aligned} p˙​×L​=−r2mk​[rr˙−r˙r]=mk[rr˙​−r2rr˙​]=mkdtd​(rr​)=mkdtdr^​,​

the last line by the quotient rule. Hence ddt(p×L−mkr^)=0\dv{}{t}\big(\vv p\times\vv L - mk\hat{\vv r}\big)=0dtd​(p×L−mkr^)=0. ■\blacksquare■ (Verified symbolically in three dimensions, componentwise, on the equations of motion.)

Identity one: A\vv AA lies in the orbital plane. Dot with L\vv LL. The first term gives (p×L)⋅L=0(\vv p\times\vv L)\cdot\vv L=0(p×L)⋅L=0 because a cross product is perpendicular to its factors; the second gives −mk r^⋅L=0-mk\,\hat{\vv r}\cdot\vv L = 0−mkr^⋅L=0 because L=r×p\vv L=\vv r\times\vv pL=r×p is perpendicular to r\vv rr. So A⋅L=0\vv A\cdot\vv L=0A⋅L=0: the vector lies in the plane of the orbit, which is why it can point at the perihelion.

Identity two: its length is fixed by EEE and LLL. Square it, using p⊥L\vv p\perp\vv Lp⊥L (so ∣p×L∣=pL\abs{\vv p\times\vv L}=pL∣p×L∣=pL) and (p×L)⋅r^=L⋅(r×p)/r=L2/r(\vv p\times\vv L)\cdot\hat{\vv r}=\vv L\cdot(\vv r\times\vv p)/r=L^{2}/r(p×L)⋅r^=L⋅(r×p)/r=L2/r:

A2=p2L2+m2k2−2mk L2r=L2 ⁣(p2−2mkr)+m2k2=2mE L2+m2k2, \begin{aligned} A^{2} &= p^{2}L^{2} + m^{2}k^{2} - 2mk\,\frac{L^{2}}{r} = L^{2}\!\left(p^{2}-\frac{2mk}{r}\right) + m^{2}k^{2}\\[4pt] &= 2mE\,L^{2} + m^{2}k^{2}, \end{aligned} A2​=p2L2+m2k2−2mkrL2​=L2(p2−r2mk​)+m2k2=2mEL2+m2k2,​

since E=p2/2m−k/rE=p^{2}/2m-k/rE=p2/2m−k/r gives p2−2mk/r=2mEp^{2}-2mk/r=2mEp2−2mk/r=2mE. So A\vv AA is not a sixth independent constant: its direction in the plane is one new number and its length is determined. Five independent constants, not six — which is exactly the count needed to fix an orbit in space completely apart from where along it the particle currently sits.

What it is. Dot A\vv AA into r\vv rr, using the cyclic property of the scalar triple product:

A⋅r=(p×L)⋅r−mkr=L⋅(r×p)−mkr=L2−mkr. \vv A\cdot\vv r = (\vv p\times\vv L)\cdot\vv r - mkr = \vv L\cdot(\vv r\times\vv p) - mkr = L^{2} - mkr. A⋅r=(p×L)⋅r−mkr=L⋅(r×p)−mkr=L2−mkr.

Writing A⋅r=Arcos⁡θ\vv A\cdot\vv r = Ar\cos\thetaA⋅r=Arcosθ with θ\thetaθ measured from the fixed direction of A\vv AA and solving for rrr:

r(θ)  =  L2/mk1+ecos⁡θ,e  ≡  Amk. r(\theta) \;=\; \frac{L^{2}/mk}{1 + e\cos\theta}, \qquad e \;\equiv\; \frac{A}{mk}. r(θ)=1+ecosθL2/mk​,e≡mkA​.

That is the polar equation of a conic of eccentricity eee — an ellipse for e<1e\lt1e<1 — with rrr smallest at θ=0\theta=0θ=0. So A\vv AA points from the focus to the perihelion, and its length is the eccentricity times mkmkmk. Its conservation is the statement that the orbit's axis never moves: Kepler ellipses close and do not precess. Adding any deviation from exact 1/r1/r1/r destroys A\vv AA and the orbit precesses — which is exactly what the λ\lambdaλ dial did to the closed orbit in §4.4's figure, and exactly what the Sun's other planets, and then general relativity, do to Mercury (Chapter 3.7).

Where is the symmetry? By §7.2 there must be one: A\vv AA has no explicit time dependence and is conserved, so {A,H}=0\{\vv A,H\}=0{A,H}=0, so the transformation A\vv AA generates leaves HHH invariant. But look at the list of §3.4 — nothing there produces A\vv AA. The reason is that the transformation generated by A\vv AA is not a motion of space at all. It mixes positions with momenta, deforming an orbit into a different orbit of the same energy — turning a circle into a thin ellipse, say. No rearrangement of the coordinates does that, which is why it is called a hidden symmetry. The Lagrangian derivation of §2 assumed the transformation acted on qqq alone and could never have found it; the phase-space picture of §7 finds it immediately, because on phase space qqq and ppp are on the same footing and there are transformations that mix them.

Now the structure. The brackets of the six conserved quantities close on themselves — this part is a computation, of exactly the kind §7.3 did by hand, only longer:

{Li,Lj}=εijkLk,{Li,Aj}=εijkAk,{Ai,Aj}=−2mH εijkLk, \{L_{i},L_{j}\}=\varepsilon_{ijk}L_{k}, \qquad \{L_{i},A_{j}\}=\varepsilon_{ijk}A_{k}, \qquad \{A_{i},A_{j}\}=-2mH\,\varepsilon_{ijk}L_{k}, {Li​,Lj​}=εijk​Lk​,{Li​,Aj​}=εijk​Ak​,{Ai​,Aj​}=−2mHεijk​Lk​,

(all three verified symbolically here.) ⚑ The identification that follows is quoted, since naming an abstract Lie algebra is Chapter 6.1's business: for bound orbits E<0E\lt0E<0 the rescaled vector D=A/−2mE\vv D=\vv A/\sqrt{-2mE}D=A/−2mE​ makes the last relation match the first. The resulting six-generator Lie algebra is that of SO(4)SO(4)SO(4) — the rotation group of four-dimensional space. The Kepler problem in three dimensions has the symmetry of rotations in four. That is the hidden symmetry, and it is why there are five constants instead of four and why the orbits close.

⚑ And the payoff arrives in Chapter 4.5. The hydrogen atom is the quantum 1/r1/r1/r problem, so it inherits this same SO(4)SO(4)SO(4). Its energy levels depend only on the principal quantum number nnn and not on the orbital angular momentum ℓ\ellℓ — the 2s2s2s and 2p2p2p states are degenerate — which looks like a numerical accident and is presented as one in most first courses. It is not an accident. It is the extra symmetry, showing up as a degeneracy, exactly as the λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 orbit in §4.4's figure showed its extra symmetry by closing.

Which is the moral, and it is worth carrying out of this chapter as a working heuristic: an unexplained coincidence in physics is usually an unrecognised symmetry. A degeneracy that "just happens", a quantity that "happens" to stay constant, a term that "happens" to cancel — each is a symmetry that has not yet been named. Looking for it is one of the most reliably productive things a physicist can do, and Chapter 6.6 is what happens when the search succeeds and Chapter 5.9 is what happens when it fails.

9 · Your turn

Problem 1 — a scaling that is a Noether symmetry

Consider a particle on the half-line x>0x\gt0x>0 with

L  =  12mx˙2  −  kx2,k>0. L \;=\; \half m\dot x^{2} \;-\; \frac{k}{x^{2}}, \qquad k\gt0. L=21​mx˙2−x2k​,k>0.

(a) Show that the combined scaling x↦ℓxx\mapsto\ell xx↦ℓx, t↦ℓ2tt\mapsto\ell^{2}tt↦ℓ2t leaves the action exactly invariant. (b) Identify KKK and τ\tauτ and use (1.4.15) to find the conserved charge. (c) Verify directly that it is conserved. (d) Why does this scaling work when §7's free-particle scaling did not?

Solution

(a) Under x′(t′)=ℓx(t)x'(t')=\ell x(t)x′(t′)=ℓx(t) with t′=ℓ2tt'=\ell^{2}tt′=ℓ2t, the velocity scales as dx′/dt′=ℓ/ℓ2⋅x˙=ℓ−1x˙\dd x'/\dd t' = \ell/\ell^{2}\cdot\dot x=\ell^{-1}\dot xdx′/dt′=ℓ/ℓ2⋅x˙=ℓ−1x˙, so the kinetic term scales by ℓ−2\ell^{-2}ℓ−2; the potential k/x′2k/x'^{2}k/x′2 scales by ℓ−2\ell^{-2}ℓ−2 as well. Both terms of LLL therefore carry the same factor ℓ−2\ell^{-2}ℓ−2, while the measure dt′=ℓ2dt\dd t'=\ell^{2}\dd tdt′=ℓ2dt carries ℓ+2\ell^{+2}ℓ+2:

S′=∫L′ dt′=∫ℓ−2L⋅ℓ2 dt=S. S' = \int L'\,\dd t' = \int \ell^{-2}L\cdot\ell^{2}\,\dd t = S. S′=∫L′dt′=∫ℓ−2L⋅ℓ2dt=S.

Exact invariance, F=0F=0F=0. (Confirmed symbolically.) The reason it works is that the two terms of LLL have the same scaling weight, and 1/x21/x^{2}1/x2 is the unique power for which they do. This is the simplest system in physics with a scale symmetry.

(b) Set ℓ=1+ϵ\ell=1+\epsilonℓ=1+ϵ. Then δx=ϵx\delta x=\epsilon xδx=ϵx and δt=2ϵt\delta t=2\epsilon tδt=2ϵt, so K=xK=xK=x and τ=2t\tau=2tτ=2t, and (1.4.15) gives

Q  =  p x−2t H  =  mxx˙  −  2t(12mx˙2+kx2). Q \;=\; p\,x - 2t\,H \;=\; m x\dot x \;-\; 2t\left(\half m\dot x^{2} + \frac{k}{x^{2}}\right). Q=px−2tH=mxx˙−2t(21​mx˙2+x2k​).

(c) The equation of motion is mx¨=−ddx ⁣(kx2)=2kx3m\ddot x = -\dv{}{x}\!\left(\dfrac{k}{x^{2}}\right) = \dfrac{2k}{x^{3}}mx¨=−dxd​(x2k​)=x32k​. Differentiate QQQ, remembering that H=EH=EH=E is itself conserved because LLL has no explicit ttt:

dQdt=mx˙2+mxx¨−2E=mx˙2+x⋅2kx3−2(12mx˙2+kx2)=0.  ✓ \dv{Q}{t} = m\dot x^{2} + mx\ddot x - 2E = m\dot x^{2} + x\cdot\frac{2k}{x^{3}} - 2\left(\half m\dot x^{2} + \frac{k}{x^{2}}\right) = 0. \;\checkmark dtdQ​=mx˙2+mxx¨−2E=mx˙2+x⋅x32k​−2(21​mx˙2+x2k​)=0.✓

Note the structure: the charge is explicitly time-dependent, like the boost charge of Worked Example 1, and for the same reason — τ\tauτ and KKK contained ttt.

(d) Because here the time was scaled too, and by exactly the amount needed to make the measure compensate the integrand. In §7's free particle only xxx was scaled, giving S↦ℓ2SS\mapsto\ell^{2}SS↦ℓ2S — the equations of motion survive (they are unchanged by an overall constant factor on SSS) but the action does not, and the theorem's hypothesis fails. The lesson is that whether a scaling is a Noether symmetry depends on how it acts on time, and finding the right relative weight is exactly what one does when constructing a scale-invariant theory.

⚑ Forward pointer: this Lagrangian is the one-dimensional prototype of a conformally invariant theory. The full symmetry is larger than the single scaling — there are three charges, closing on the algebra of SL(2,R)SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) — and the two-dimensional version of the same structure, with infinitely many charges instead of three, is what makes string theory calculable in Chapter 7.2.

Problem 2 — a particle on a surface of revolution

A particle of mass mmm slides without friction on the surface obtained by rotating the curve ρ=R(z)\rho=R(z)ρ=R(z) about the zzz-axis, with no potential (V=0V=0V=0). Using cylindrical coordinates (ρ,φ,z)(\rho,\varphi,z)(ρ,φ,z):

(a) Write LLL on the surface. (b) Identify the symmetry and its Noether charge. (c) Use it to reduce the motion to a single first-order equation for z(t)z(t)z(t), i.e. to a quadrature. (d) Show that the charge is equivalent to Clairaut's relation: Rsin⁡ψR\sin\psiRsinψ is constant, where ψ\psiψ is the angle between the trajectory and the local meridian.

Solution

(a) In cylindrical coordinates the squared speed is ρ˙2+ρ2φ˙2+z˙2\dot\rho^{2}+\rho^{2}\dot\varphi^{2}+\dot z^{2}ρ˙​2+ρ2φ˙​2+z˙2. On the surface ρ=R(z)\rho=R(z)ρ=R(z), so ρ˙=R′(z)z˙\dot\rho=R'(z)\dot zρ˙​=R′(z)z˙ and

L  =  12m[(1+R′(z)2)z˙2  +  R(z)2φ˙2]. L \;=\; \half m\Big[\big(1+R'(z)^{2}\big)\dot z^{2} \;+\; R(z)^{2}\dot\varphi^{2}\Big]. L=21​m[(1+R′(z)2)z˙2+R(z)2φ˙​2].

Two coordinates, because imposing the constraint by choosing coordinates is exactly what Chapter 1.2 §6 recommended.

(b) φ\varphiφ does not appear in LLL — the surface is unchanged by rotating about its axis, which is the symmetry δφ=ϵ\delta\varphi=\epsilonδφ=ϵ, Kφ=1K_{\varphi}=1Kφ​=1, τ=0\tau=0τ=0, F=0F=0F=0. So

Q  =  ∂L∂φ˙  =  m R(z)2 φ˙  ≡  ℓ  =  constant, Q \;=\; \pdv{L}{\dot\varphi} \;=\; m\,R(z)^{2}\,\dot\varphi \;\equiv\; \ell \;=\; \text{constant,} Q=∂φ˙​∂L​=mR(z)2φ˙​≡ℓ=constant,

the angular momentum about the axis. (This is §3.2's cyclic-coordinate case, and it is what Chapter 1.2 saw in polar coordinates without a name for it.)

(c) LLL has no explicit ttt, so E=12m[(1+R′2)z˙2+R2φ˙2]E=\half m[(1+R'^{2})\dot z^{2}+R^{2}\dot\varphi^{2}]E=21​m[(1+R′2)z˙2+R2φ˙​2] is conserved as well. Eliminate φ˙=ℓ/(mR2)\dot\varphi=\ell/(mR^{2})φ˙​=ℓ/(mR2):

E  =  12m(1+R′2)z˙2  +  ℓ22mR(z)2⏟Veff(z). E \;=\; \half m\big(1+R'^{2}\big)\dot z^{2} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\ell^{2}}{2mR(z)^{2}}}_{V_{\rm eff}(z)}. E=21​m(1+R′2)z˙2+Veff​(z)2mR(z)2ℓ2​​​.

Two conserved quantities have reduced two coupled second-order equations to one first-order equation, which separates:

t−t0  =  ∫m(1+R′(z)2)2(E−ℓ2/2mR(z)2)  dz, t - t_{0} \;=\; \int \sqrt{\frac{m\big(1+R'(z)^{2}\big)}{2\big(E - \ell^{2}/2mR(z)^{2}\big)}}\;\dd z, t−t0​=∫2(E−ℓ2/2mR(z)2)m(1+R′(z)2)​​dz,

and then φ(t)\varphi(t)φ(t) follows by integrating φ˙=ℓ/mR2\dot\varphi=\ell/mR^{2}φ˙​=ℓ/mR2. The problem is solved by quadrature. Every conserved quantity buys one integration; two of them turn a two-degree-of-freedom problem into arithmetic.

Note also that Veff∝1/R2V_{\rm eff}\propto1/R^{2}Veff​∝1/R2 acts as a barrier wherever the surface narrows: a particle with ℓ≠0\ell\neq0ℓ=0 cannot reach a neck of radius smaller than Rmin⁡=ℓ/2mER_{\min}=\ell/\sqrt{2mE}Rmin​=ℓ/2mE​. That is the centrifugal barrier, arriving here as a consequence of a symmetry rather than as a fictitious force.

(d) With V=0V=0V=0 the speed vvv is constant (energy conservation). Decompose the velocity into a component along the local circle of latitude, vφ=Rφ˙v_{\varphi}=R\dot\varphivφ​=Rφ˙​, and one along the meridian. If ψ\psiψ is the angle between the trajectory and the meridian, then sin⁡ψ=vφ/v\sin\psi = v_{\varphi}/vsinψ=vφ​/v, so

ℓ=mR2φ˙=mR vφ=m v Rsin⁡ψ⟹Rsin⁡ψ=constant. \ell = mR^{2}\dot\varphi = mR\,v_{\varphi} = m\,v\,R\sin\psi \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad R\sin\psi = \text{constant}. ℓ=mR2φ˙​=mRvφ​=mvRsinψ⟹Rsinψ=constant.

This is Clairaut's relation, and it is what Chapter 1.2's grind box on spherical geodesics found by integrating the Euler–Lagrange equation and then remarked was "Noether's theorem arriving three chapters early disguised as cartography". Here is the general version: on any surface of revolution, the geodesics obey Rsin⁡ψ=R\sin\psi=Rsinψ= constant because the surface has an axial symmetry. It is also the reason a great-circle route from London to Tokyo goes over the Arctic — the path must turn toward the axis as RRR decreases to keep the product fixed.

Problem 3 — the current of a complex field, and what the charge is

For the field theory of (1.4.37), derive the Noether current for the global phase symmetry from scratch (do not quote §6.2), and evaluate the charge density j0j^{0}j0 on the plane-wave solution ϕ=Ne−i(Et−p⋅x)\phi=N\ee^{-\ii(Et-\vv p\cdot\vv x)}ϕ=Ne−i(Et−p⋅x) with NNN real. Then evaluate it on the complex-conjugate solution ϕ∗\phi^{*}ϕ∗ and say what the sign means.

Solution

Setup. Treat ϕ\phiϕ and ϕ∗\phi^{*}ϕ∗ as two independent fields. Writing L=gμν∂μϕ∗∂νϕ−m2ϕ∗ϕ\mathcal{L}=g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}\phi^{*}\partial_{\nu}\phi - m^{2}\phi^{*}\phiL=gμν∂μ​ϕ∗∂ν​ϕ−m2ϕ∗ϕ,

∂L∂(∂μϕ)=∂μϕ∗,∂L∂(∂μϕ∗)=∂μϕ. \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)} = \partial^{\mu}\phi^{*}, \qquad \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi^{*})} = \partial^{\mu}\phi. ∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​=∂μϕ∗,∂(∂μ​ϕ∗)∂L​=∂μϕ.

The transformation. ϕ→eiαϕ\phi\to\ee^{\ii\alpha}\phiϕ→eiαϕ gives, to first order in ϵ=α\epsilon=\alphaϵ=α,

δϕ=iα ϕ  ⇒  Kϕ=iϕ,δϕ∗=−iα ϕ∗  ⇒  Kϕ∗=−iϕ∗. \delta\phi = \ii\alpha\,\phi \;\Rightarrow\; K_{\phi}=\ii\phi, \qquad \delta\phi^{*} = -\ii\alpha\,\phi^{*} \;\Rightarrow\; K_{\phi^{*}}=-\ii\phi^{*}. δϕ=iαϕ⇒Kϕ​=iϕ,δϕ∗=−iαϕ∗⇒Kϕ∗​=−iϕ∗.

L\mathcal{L}L pairs each ϕ\phiϕ with a ϕ∗\phi^{*}ϕ∗, so the phases cancel and δL=0\delta\mathcal{L}=0δL=0 exactly: Fμ=0F^{\mu}=0Fμ=0.

The current. Sum (1.4.34) over the two fields:

jμ=∂μϕ∗ (iϕ)+∂μϕ (−iϕ∗)=i(ϕ ∂μϕ∗−ϕ∗∂μϕ). j^{\mu} = \partial^{\mu}\phi^{*}\,(\ii\phi) + \partial^{\mu}\phi\,(-\ii\phi^{*}) = \ii\big(\phi\,\partial^{\mu}\phi^{*} - \phi^{*}\partial^{\mu}\phi\big). jμ=∂μϕ∗(iϕ)+∂μϕ(−iϕ∗)=i(ϕ∂μϕ∗−ϕ∗∂μϕ).

On a plane wave. With ϕ=Ne−i(Et−p⋅x)\phi = N\ee^{-\ii(Et-\vv p\cdot\vv x)}ϕ=Ne−i(Et−p⋅x) we have ∂0ϕ=∂tϕ=−iEϕ\partial^{0}\phi=\partial_{t}\phi=-\ii E\phi∂0ϕ=∂t​ϕ=−iEϕ and ∂0ϕ∗=+iEϕ∗\partial^{0}\phi^{*}=+\ii E\phi^{*}∂0ϕ∗=+iEϕ∗, so

j0=i(ϕ (iEϕ∗)−ϕ∗(−iEϕ))=i(2iE∣ϕ∣2)=−2EN2. j^{0} = \ii\Big(\phi\,(\ii E\phi^{*}) - \phi^{*}(-\ii E\phi)\Big) = \ii\big(2\ii E\abs{\phi}^{2}\big) = -2EN^{2}. j0=i(ϕ(iEϕ∗)−ϕ∗(−iEϕ))=i(2iE∣ϕ∣2)=−2EN2.

The conjugate solution. ϕ∗=Ne+i(Et−p⋅x)\phi^{*}=N\ee^{+\ii(Et-\vv p\cdot\vv x)}ϕ∗=Ne+i(Et−p⋅x) is also a solution of □ϕ=−m2ϕ\Box\phi=-m^{2}\phi□ϕ=−m2ϕ, and running the same computation gives j0=+2EN2j^{0}=+2EN^{2}j0=+2EN2: the same magnitude, opposite sign.

What it means. A complex field carries a conserved charge, and the field has two families of solutions carrying that charge with opposite signs and equal magnitude. A real field has no such symmetry — there is no phase to rotate — and therefore no conserved charge at all. So: a field carries charge if and only if it is complex. Multiplying jμj^{\mu}jμ by the constant −q-q−q (allowed, since any constant multiple of a conserved current is conserved) makes the first solution carry charge +q+q+q per unit 2EN22EN^{2}2EN2 and the second −q-q−q.

⚑ Forward: after quantisation in Chapter 5.3 the two families become particles and antiparticles. Antimatter is not an extra postulate — it is the second sign of the Noether charge of a U(1)U(1)U(1) symmetry, and it exists for exactly the same reason the charge does. A neutral particle like the photon is described by a real field precisely because it has no U(1)U(1)U(1) charge to carry, and is therefore its own antiparticle.

Problem 4 — a symmetry with no charge, and Kepler's third law

For the Kepler Lagrangian L=12m∣r˙∣2+k/rL=\half m\abs{\dot{\vv r}}^{2}+k/rL=21​m∣r˙∣2+k/r, consider the scaling

r  ⟼  ℓ r,t  ⟼  ℓ3/2 t. \vv r \;\longmapsto\; \ell\,\vv r, \qquad t \;\longmapsto\; \ell^{3/2}\,t. r⟼ℓr,t⟼ℓ3/2t.

(a) Show that it maps solutions to solutions. (b) Show that it is not a symmetry of the action, and that the would-be Noether charge is not conserved. (c) What does the transformation give you instead? (d) Contrast with Problem 1.

Solution

(a) The equation of motion is mr¨=−kr/r3m\ddot{\vv r} = -k\vv r/r^{3}mr¨=−kr/r3. Under the scaling, the left side picks up ℓ/ℓ3=ℓ−2\ell/\ell^{3}=\ell^{-2}ℓ/ℓ3=ℓ−2 and the right side picks up ℓ/ℓ3=ℓ−2\ell/\ell^{3}=\ell^{-2}ℓ/ℓ3=ℓ−2 as well. Both sides scale identically, so the equation is unchanged and every solution maps to a solution.

(b) Now scale the action. The velocity scales by ℓ/ℓ3/2=ℓ−1/2\ell/\ell^{3/2}=\ell^{-1/2}ℓ/ℓ3/2=ℓ−1/2, so T↦ℓ−1TT\mapsto\ell^{-1}TT↦ℓ−1T; the potential k/r↦ℓ−1k/rk/r\mapsto\ell^{-1}k/rk/r↦ℓ−1k/r. Both terms of LLL carry ℓ−1\ell^{-1}ℓ−1, while dt\dd tdt carries ℓ3/2\ell^{3/2}ℓ3/2, so

S  ⟼  ℓ−1⋅ℓ3/2 S  =  ℓ1/2 S  ≠  S. S \;\longmapsto\; \ell^{-1}\cdot\ell^{3/2}\,S \;=\; \ell^{1/2}\,S \;\neq\; S. S⟼ℓ−1⋅ℓ3/2S=ℓ1/2S=S.

Not invariant, and not invariant up to a boundary term either — the change is proportional to SSS itself, which is not the integral of a total derivative for a general path. The hypothesis of §1.2 fails.

Test the conclusion. With ℓ=1+ϵ\ell=1+\epsilonℓ=1+ϵ the would-be generators are K=r\vv K=\vv rK=r and τ=32t\tau=\tfrac32tτ=23​t, so (1.4.15) would offer

Q  =?  p⋅r−32tE. Q \;\overset{?}{=}\; \vv p\cdot\vv r - \tfrac32 tE. Q=?p⋅r−23​tE.

Differentiate along a solution, using ddt(p⋅r)=∣p∣2/m+r⋅p˙=2T−k/r\dv{}{t}(\vv p\cdot\vv r)=\abs{\vv p}^{2}/m+\vv r\cdot\dot{\vv p} = 2T - k/rdtd​(p⋅r)=∣p∣2/m+r⋅p˙​=2T−k/r (the last step because r⋅p˙=−k/r\vv r\cdot\dot{\vv p}=-k/rr⋅p˙​=−k/r):

dQdt=2T−kr−32E=2T−kr−32(T−kr)=12(T+kr)  =  12 L  ≠  0. \dv{Q}{t} = 2T - \frac{k}{r} - \tfrac32E = 2T - \frac{k}{r} - \tfrac32\left(T - \frac{k}{r}\right) = \half\left(T + \frac{k}{r}\right) \;=\; \half\,L \;\neq\; 0. dtdQ​=2T−rk​−23​E=2T−rk​−23​(T−rk​)=21​(T+rk​)=21​L=0.

Not conserved — and not even conserved on average: over one closed orbit p⋅r\vv p\cdot\vv rp⋅r returns to its starting value, so ⟨dQdt⟩=−32E≠0\avg{\dv{Q}{t}} = -\tfrac32 E \neq 0⟨dtdQ​⟩=−23​E=0 for a bound orbit. What does average to zero is the simpler combination G=p⋅rG=\vv p\cdot\vv rG=p⋅r on its own, whose rate is dGdt=2T−k/r\dv{G}{t}=2T-k/rdtdG​=2T−k/r; setting its average to zero gives

⟨2T⟩  =  ⟨k/r⟩, \avg{2T} \;=\; \avg{k/r}, ⟨2T⟩=⟨k/r⟩,

the virial theorem. That is the residue a non-symmetry leaves behind: not a constant, but a relation between time-averages.

(c) The transformation relates different solutions rather than constraining a single one. Take any orbit, scale all lengths by ℓ\ellℓ and all times by ℓ3/2\ell^{3/2}ℓ3/2, and you get another legitimate orbit. Since the semi-major axis scales as a↦ℓaa\mapsto\ell aa↦ℓa and the period as T↦ℓ3/2TT\mapsto\ell^{3/2}TT↦ℓ3/2T, the combination

T2a3  ⟼  ℓ3T2ℓ3a3  =  T2a3 \frac{T^{2}}{a^{3}} \;\longmapsto\; \frac{\ell^{3}T^{2}}{\ell^{3}a^{3}} \;=\; \frac{T^{2}}{a^{3}} a3T2​⟼ℓ3a3ℓ3T2​=a3T2​

is the same for every orbit. That is Kepler's third law, obtained without solving the equations of motion at all — from a symmetry that has no Noether charge. Symmetries of the equations of motion are not useless; they simply produce a different kind of information: relations between solutions, not constants along one.

(d) The two problems differ in exactly one respect: whether the time-scaling exponent is the one that makes ∫L dt\int L\,\dd t∫Ldt balance. In Problem 1, LLL scaled by ℓ−2\ell^{-2}ℓ−2 and dt\dd tdt by ℓ+2\ell^{+2}ℓ+2 — they cancel, giving a Noether charge. Here LLL scales by ℓ−1\ell^{-1}ℓ−1 and dt\dd tdt by ℓ3/2\ell^{3/2}ℓ3/2 — they do not, and there is none. Same kind of transformation, same kind of system, and the presence or absence of a conservation law turns on a single exponent. That is a useful reminder that "is this a symmetry?" is a question about the action, and can only be answered by computing.

The brick you just laid

You can now convert symmetry into conservation, in either direction, by formula. Given a transformation δqi=ϵKi\delta q_{i}=\epsilon K_{i}δqi​=ϵKi​, δt=ϵτ\delta t=\epsilon\tauδt=ϵτ under which the action is invariant up to a boundary term ϵF\epsilon FϵF, the quantity Q=∑ipiKi−Hτ−FQ=\sum_{i}p_{i}K_{i}-H\tau-FQ=∑i​pi​Ki​−Hτ−F is constant along solutions (1.4.15); and given a conserved QQQ, the bracket δf=ϵ{f,Q}\delta f=\epsilon\{f,Q\}δf=ϵ{f,Q} hands the symmetry back. The proof was four steps — variations commute with d/dt\dd/\dd td/dt, expand by the chain rule, substitute the Euler–Lagrange equation, recognise a total derivative — and the only subtlety worth remembering is that the hypothesis is off shell while the conclusion is on shell.

From the one formula came energy, momentum, angular momentum, the uniform motion of the centre of mass, and electric charge. You saw conservation fail, on screen, in exactly the component whose symmetry you broke, at exactly the predicted rate. You saw that discrete symmetries give no current, that in fields the theorem upgrades to a local statement — Chapter 0.7's continuity equation — and that an unexplained degeneracy is usually a symmetry nobody has named yet.

Where this gets spent. Chapter 2.5 applies it to spacetime translations in Minkowski space and gets four-momentum conservation as a single relation. Chapter 3.5 geometrises it: Killing vectors are Noether generators written as vector fields on a manifold, and Chapter 3.6 finds ∇μTμν=0\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}=0∇μ​Tμν=0 falling out of the invariance of the Einstein–Hilbert action under coordinate changes. Chapter 5.2 runs §6 in earnest for relativistic fields and constructs the energy–momentum tensor. Chapter 6.3 takes §6.2's U(1)U(1)U(1), makes α\alphaα depend on position, and out comes electromagnetism; Chapter 6.7 does it with the full Standard Model group. And Chapter 4.7 finds §7's bracket algebra again with commutators, which is where spin comes from.

Part I, closed. Four chapters ago mechanics was a list of forces, one per interaction, each resolved into components in a coordinate system chosen for convenience. It is now four objects: a single scalar LLL; the condition δS=0\delta S=0δS=0 that turns it into equations of motion; a bracket { ,}\{\,,\}{,} that turns phase-space functions into motions; and a theorem converting symmetry into conservation. Nothing in that list mentions gravity, or electrons, or fields, or any particular physics at all — which is the point, because every remaining part of this book is that same package applied to a different symmetry group. Lorentz transformations in Part II. Diffeomorphisms — arbitrary smooth coordinate changes — in Part III. Unitary phase rotations, first global and then local, in Parts IV to VI. Conformal transformations of a two-dimensional worldsheet in Part VII. You now have the whole method. What remains is to learn the groups.
